slides.heading: How Brain-Computer Interfaces Work
slides.body: The technology turning thoughts into action — and reshaping human potential

slides.heading: What Is a BCI?
slides.body: A brain-computer interface (BCI) is a direct communication pathway between the brain and an external device. It reads electrical signals from neurons and translates them into commands — no muscles required.

slides.heading: Reading the Brain's Signals
slides.body: Neurons fire by exchanging ions, generating tiny electrical pulses called action potentials. BCIs detect these signals using electrodes placed on or inside the skull, picking up patterns that correspond to intended movements or thoughts.

slides.heading: Non-Invasive vs. Invasive
slides.body: EEG headsets sit on the scalp and are safe but noisy. Invasive implants, like Neuralink's chip, sit directly on the cortex and capture far cleaner, higher-resolution signals — at the cost of surgery and long-term biocompatibility.

slides.heading: Decoding Intent with AI
slides.body: Raw neural data is meaningless without decoding. Machine learning models — trained on thousands of signal-action pairs — learn to map brain patterns to intended outputs like cursor movement, text, or robotic arm control.

slides.heading: Real-World Breakthroughs
slides.body: Paralyzed patients have used BCIs to type at 90 characters per minute using only their thoughts. In 2024, a Neuralink recipient played chess and browsed the web hands-free, demonstrating real-world viability.

slides.heading: Bidirectional Interfaces
slides.body: Next-generation BCIs don't just read — they write. By stimulating specific neurons, they can restore lost sensations, suppress seizures, or even bypass spinal injuries to reconnect brain signals directly to muscles.

slides.heading: The Challenges Ahead
slides.body: Long-term implants face scar tissue buildup that degrades signal quality over months. Wireless data transmission, battery life, and preventing infection remain major engineering hurdles before BCIs become widely available.

slides.heading: Ethics and Privacy
slides.body: Brain data is the most intimate data imaginable. Who owns your neural signals? Can employers or insurers demand access? BCIs raise urgent questions about cognitive liberty, mental privacy, and the risk of hacking the mind.

slides.heading: The Mind-Machine Future
slides.body: BCIs could restore movement, speech, and sight to millions — and one day blur the line between human cognition and computing. The question isn't if, but how carefully we build this bridge.
